To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

specific afferent renal denervation (A-RDN), but not sham denervation, restores neuronal nitric oxide syntheses (nNOS)-positive cells and nNOS protein in the paraventicular nucleus (PV) of rats with chronic heart failure (H).
specific renal denervation prevents reduction in neuronal nitric oxide in the paravertebral nucleus of rats with chronic heart failure.
specific afferent renal denervation restores nNOS within the paraventricual nucleus, which in turn reduces sympathetic drive during chronic hear failure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the contribution of the intact afferent innervation from the kidney to sympathetic overdrive in CHF.
the role of afferent nerves in the sympathetic outflow within PVN during CHF.
the role of afferent nerves in the regulation of nNOS within the PVN and sympathetic drive in CHFs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
afferent renal nerve activation is an important mechanism in the development of sympathetic activation in CHF.
afferent renal denervation prevents reduction of neuronal nitric oxide in the paraventrical nucleus and reduces sympathetic drive in chronic heart failure.
A-RDN prevents the reduction in nNOS in PVN in CHF rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
afferent renal denervation attenuates sympathetic drive by restoring nNOS in PVN in CHF.
A-RDN prevents the reduction in nNOS in PVN and restores the nNOS activity in PVN, which attenuates the sympathoadrenal activation in CHF rats.
afferent renal denervation prevents reduction in neuronal nitric oxide in the paraventral nucleus and attenuates sympathetic outflow during chronic heart failure.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the afferent renal nerve activity is elevated in heart failure rats and this may highlight a crucial mechanism arising from the kidneys in the maintenance of the sympathetic overactivity in heart failure rats.
renal nerves contribute to sympathoexcitation in CHF and that renal denervation may be a useful therapeutic approach in CHF.
the sympathetic drive in CHFs is not only dependent on the efferent renal nerves but also on the afferent renal nerve activity.
